stature.source: FEIS: typically about 30 m, occasionally to about 50 m; no record tree read; read 2026-11-04

targets.from: judgement values from the drafter's reading of the sources and knowledge of the species (2026-11-04), no photographs measured; to be replaced by photo measurements: a tall, straight grey trunk, clear for its lower half in stands (FEIS), carrying a narrow, open, upswept crown; broad and open on a lone tree on a gravel bar

young.note: a fast sapling thicket on a fresh gravel bar, smooth greenish-grey bark

veteran.note: a river-bar giant with deeply furrowed grey bark and a broken, open crown of a few huge upswept limbs; often an eagle's perch

description: The tallest broadleaf tree of the Northwest, 30-45 m on the Hoh and Queets bars, with a straight grey trunk that furrows deeply with age and a narrow, open crown. Its big, pointed leaves are dark glossy green above and silvery below, flickering in the river wind, and its sticky spring buds scent the valley.

season_notes.winter: Bare grey crowns along the river; resinous buds.
season_notes.spring: Sweet balsam smell of the buds; catkins before the leaves, April-May.
season_notes.summer: In June the female catkins release white cotton that drifts over the gravel bars and eddies.
season_notes.fall: Leaves turn yellow and fall September-October.

riparian.water: A tree of the big rivers: gravel bars, floodplains and young terraces where floods lay down fresh, wet sand and gravel for its seed (FEIS).

range.where: the floodplains of the Hoh, Queets, Quinault, Elwha and Dungeness; Alaska to southern California and inland to the Rockies

notes: Grown from Fremont cottonwood (same genus) as a taller, narrower tree with a higher crown base and darker, glossier leaves. Leaves 7-12 cm (to 20 on sprouts), ovate to deltoid with a pointed tip, dark green above, whitish-silvery below (drafter's knowledge; FEIS does not describe them); the silver undersides flickering in wind are not drawn. FEIS: Roosevelt elk took about 9% of their diet from it in one Olympic National Park study, and use it for cover; deer use it mainly for cover; beavers eat it and build with it; ruffed grouse eat the buds; bald eagles, ospreys and great blue herons nest and perch in it. Only the deer, red-tailed hawk and raven are in the animal library. The cotton drifting in June would need a particle effect.
